newsitem.title: USA: Pennsylvania gov. sets plan to sell liquor stores.
newsitem.headline: Pennsylvania gov. sets plan to sell liquor stores.

text.p: Gov. Tom Ridge on Wednesday unveiled a plan to sell Pennsylvania's 64-year-old state liquor-store system, saying the proposal would raise $3.2 billion over 10 years and benefit consumers.
"Government is here to serve the people, not to serve them alcohol," Ridge told a news conference. "It's time to sell Pennsylvania's state liquor stores."

The plan, which requires approval by the state Legislature, falls short of a complete privatization of the state's alcohol sales system, one of the last two in the nation with total control over liquor sales.
The state would retain control over wholesale sales but would allow corporations and individuals to bid on the franchise rights to 757 retail wine and spirit stores.

That represents the peak number of outlets within the state-store system, reached in the mid-1970s. Franchises would be sold to the highest "responsible' bidder." Ownership is limited to 10 percent of the total stores statewide and 40 percent in any single county.
The proposal would prohibit the sale of liquor, wine or beer in grocery and convenience stores, and in pharmacies.
The current system of selling beer through private distributorships would remain intact. Despite those restrictions, Ridge said the plan would help consumers by offering improved value and service.
"Pennsylvanians have told us they want better hours, service, selection and prices. This plan aims to produce them," he said.
Ridge estimated his proposal would generate $3.2 billion duing the first 10 years through franchise fees and subsequent annual transfers.
To be sure, the net gain from privatization -- the money available for spending -- would be $605 million, after subtracting projected earnings from the existing system.

Aside from transition costs and increased funds for alcohol enforcement and education, Ridge proposed spending the proceeds on a scholarship fund for high school seniors and a Better Communities Fund, the interest from which would be used to help Pennsylvania communities build such local projects as zoos, aquariums and industrial parks.
The Legislature would have to approve any such projects.

Ridge's plan calls for investing $388 million over 10 years in the communities fund, including an immediate deposit of $207 million in a permanent endowment. Interest from the endowment and the other funds would generate an estimated $579 million for projects over the next 10 years. The projects would be funded through a bond issue.

Ridge attempted to allay the fears of state-store workers, whose union has vehemently opposed the sale. He proposed a tax credit of $2,000 per worker for employers who hire former state store workers.

The governor wants to increase spending on enforcement of state liquor laws and alcohol education for minors by almost $58 million over 10 years. The proposal also calls for harsher penalties for violations of alcohol sales regulations.

Under the plan, franchisees would pay a large lump sum upfront and then annual fees for 10 years. At the end of the 10-year period, a rebidding process would take place. Current franchisees would be able to retain their franchise rights without rebidding if they meet certain financial criteria.
Opponents of privatization have warned that giving up state control will lead to increased alcohol consumption, underage drinking and alcohol-related accidents and fatalities.
Pennsylvania and Utah are the only states that still directly control the distribution and sale of liquor and wine.
